title: Stable curves have faithful action on their full multidegree-zero Picard group
statement: Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure], let $g\geq2$, and let $C/k$ be a stable unpointed genus-$g$ curve [def-sfb-stable-pointed-moduli-groupoids], allowing singular and reducible curves. Let $\operatorname{Pic}^0(C)$ be the group, under tensor product, of isomorphism classes of invertible $\mathcal O_C$-modules [def-sc-invertible-module] whose degree on every irreducible component is zero; degree is computed after pullback to that component's normalization. If $a:C\xrightarrow{\sim}C$ is a $k$-automorphism and $a^*[L]=[L]$ for every $[L]\in\operatorname{Pic}^0(C)$, then $a=\operatorname{id}_C$. There is no restriction on the characteristic or on the order of $a$.

source.place: Theorem 1.13, printed pp.85–87, with Lemmas 1.14–1.17; the theorem concerns the ordinary group of degree-zero-on-each-component invertible sheaves and includes reducible stable curves. Local PDF WANTED; primary PDF read online.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-nodal-component-picard-gluing] to $C$: the stable-curve definition gives a connected projective reduced nodal curve. Write $\Gamma$ for its component-intersection multigraph and $\sigma$ for the action of $a$ on it. Restriction $r$ is surjective and equivariant. Since $a^*$ is identity on its source, it is identity on $\prod_v\operatorname{Pic}^0(C_v)$. If $\operatorname{Pic}^0(C_v)$ contains a nonidentity element, put that element in the $v$-factor and identities in all other factors; its support is the singleton $\{v\}$, so identity on the product forces $\sigma(v)=v$.

source.place: Lemma 1.17, component restriction and fixed vertices

proof.text: Every vertex of degree at most two is fixed. Indeed, by the previous step a moved vertex would have trivial $\operatorname{Pic}^0(C_v)$; [lem-sfb-nodal-component-picard-gluing] then says $C_v\simeq\mathbf P^1_k$. Such a component has no self-nodes. Its special points in the unpointed stable-curve definition are precisely the distinct intersection nodes with other components. Stability requires at least three of them, contradicting degree at most two.

The injection $\iota$ in [lem-sfb-nodal-component-picard-gluing] is equivariant, so precomposition by $\sigma_*$ fixes every homomorphism $H_1(\Gamma,\mathbf Z)\to k^*$. This implies $\sigma_*=1$: if $h-\sigma_*h\ne0$ in the subgroup $H_1\subset\mathbf Z^E$, choose an edge coordinate with nonzero integer value $n$. Choose $z\in k^*$ with $z^n\ne1$ (a nonzero polynomial has finitely many roots and $k$ is infinite), and restrict the homomorphism $(m_e)_e\mapsto z^{m_e}$ to $H_1$. It distinguishes $h$ and $\sigma_*h$, a contradiction. Thus [lem-sfb-finite-graph-homology-rigidity], using the low-degree fixed vertices already proved, makes $\sigma$ identity on vertices and edges.

source.place: Lemma 1.17(iii) and graph argument on pp.86–87

proof.text: Consequently $a$ preserves each reduced component $Y=C_v$ and fixes each intersection node on it. Restriction surjectivity in [lem-sfb-nodal-component-picard-gluing] shows $b=a|_Y$ acts identically on $\operatorname{Pic}^0(Y)$. Apply [lem-sfb-integral-nodal-picard-normalization-action]: on the smooth projective normalization $\nu:\widetilde Y\to Y$, the lift $\widetilde b$ acts identically on $\operatorname{Pic}^0(\widetilde Y)$ and fixes every branch above a self-node. A node joining $Y$ to another component is a smooth point of $Y$ with a single preimage in $\widetilde Y$; equivariance of $\nu$ and its unique lift therefore fix that preimage too. Hence every special point on $\widetilde Y$ is fixed.

If $\widetilde Y$ has genus at least two, let $J$ be its smooth separated Picard-zero variety supplied by [sk-thm-picard-main]. The induced group automorphism $a_{\widetilde b}$ from [lem-sfb-curve-polarized-jacobian-faithfulness] is identity on all $J(k)=\operatorname{Pic}^0(\widetilde Y)$ by the preceding step. These points are dense by [lem-pc-rational-points-dense], since $k$ is algebraically closed and $J$ is smooth. The equalizer with $\operatorname{id}_J$ is a closed subscheme because $J$ is separated. Its underlying closed set contains the dense rational points, hence is all of $J$; its ideal is contained in the nilradical and is zero because $J$ is reduced. Thus $a_{\widetilde b}=\operatorname{id}_J$, and the injectivity assertion of [lem-sfb-curve-polarized-jacobian-faithfulness] gives $\widetilde b=\operatorname{id}_{\widetilde Y}$.

source.place: Lemma 1.15(a); smooth-case input via the existing Jacobian faithfulness node

proof.text: If $\widetilde Y$ has genus one, stability gives at least one special point and it was fixed in step 4. The genus-one assertion of [lem-sfb-low-genus-pointed-automorphism-rigidity], together with identity on $\operatorname{Pic}^0(\widetilde Y)$, gives $\widetilde b=\operatorname{id}$. If its genus is zero, stability gives three distinct special points, all fixed; the genus-zero assertion of the same node again gives $\widetilde b=\operatorname{id}$. These alternatives and step 5 exhaust the nonnegative genus of every normalized component.

It follows that $a$ is identity on the disjoint union of all normalized components, and therefore on $C$. Explicitly, on the underlying points the normalization is surjective, so $a$ fixes every point. For an affine open $U\subset C$, pullback of functions to the normalizations of its reduced components is injective: an element vanishing on each of their function fields belongs to every minimal prime of $\mathcal O_C(U)$ and is zero because $C$ is reduced. The identity after normalization then forces $a^*f=f$ on every $U$. Thus the scheme automorphism is $\operatorname{id}_C$. The argument never restricts the characteristic or the order of $a$.
